cells.tense: Right now you are down in the pattern, and you are still beside someone.
cells.ask: Let one person tell you what happened to them today, and stay quiet long enough to notice how it sits in you before you answer.
cells.core:
You go down into a question all the way, past the useful explanations, and you come back up still able to stand next to someone. Most people who go that deep come back odd or far off. You come back even, and that evenness holds on its own rather than coming from the talk around you.

When someone you're with tells you something true, your reaction stops at you. Their feeling informs you without taking you over, and they can feel the difference, even if they couldn't say what it is.

That's ordinary and it isn't cheap. One small experiment is open: take a step further into feeling with another person without borrowing their mood to get there.

cells.verb: going down through pattern until thinking meets its limit
cells.place: in the room where feeling with another gets its footing

cells.tense: You are already living in the conversation you haven't had yet.
cells.ask: Say your thought to one person this week in one or two plain sentences and stop, letting it land or not.
cells.core:
You go down into what someone is feeling and come back holding the whole shape of it, and then you start telling them what it means. You have thought it through so far ahead that the explanation arrives before they have felt anything, and you call it being useful.

But here's what happens on the other side: they stop telling you things. Not because you're wrong — you're often right — but because being explained to is not the same as being met.

The depth itself isn't the problem. It's the speed of bringing it back up. You can say what you see in one sentence and leave the rest rolled up.

cells.tense: Standing at a door that is already behind you, you still look back at it now and then.
cells.ask: Tell one person a story from your life that matters to you, and let them feel it with you without checking whether you got it right.
cells.core:
You have less to give the person in front of you, and it's not because you stopped caring. Feeling with someone stopped being the thing you do, so now you wish people well from a distance or hand them advice instead of attention.

You still see exactly what someone needs. You just don't move toward it anymore. The moving toward someone is what went quiet, and the depth has become the place you go on your own.

Walking one story into the light with another person is how this part of you re-enters. Let another person's response carry some of what you've been holding alone.
cells.sheetLine: You still see what people need. You just don't move toward it.

cells.tense: The current of feeling with people is running, and you're calling it something else.
cells.ask: Tell one person how their day is landing in you, and say it's yours to feel rather than a read on their situation.
cells.core:
You are already receiving people. You notice the temperature in a room, you adjust before anyone asks, you feel another's day in your body without deciding to. That's happening now, on its own.

But in the story you tell about yourself, you're practical or low-maintenance, or you say you're just not very emotional. Those are names for a settled kind of feeling you don't think counts. The line between you and another person's day has been running this whole time, and it hasn't been named as yours.

Feeling with someone and staying on your own footing at once is what you do, not a mode you kind of have. One plain sentence of ownership brings it back inside your own account of yourself.
cells.sheetLine: You already feel with people. You call it staying practical.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person withholds feeling; it says the well has run dry — an empty seat, not a defended one. The reader might object that they still show up for people, and that is likely true; the ask survives being wrong because telling a story to another person works even for someone who is already open. The sentence that serves the writer is the Balancer's 'that's ordinary' closing — lovely, but it flatters the reader instead of footing them.
